title: “They owe me.” What’s wrong with this belief?
description: This article explores the “they owe me” mindset—a pattern where people expect the world to revolve around them and cater to all their needs. The author explains how this mindset develops in childhood, provides examples of how it manifests in adult life, and describes the negative consequences, including frustration, relationship tension, and a loss of independence. Finally, it suggests the importance of accepting the world as it is and understanding that there is room in it not just for us, but for others as well.

texts: “They owe me” is a trap that many fall into, believing the world revolves around them.
People with this mindset often expect others to agree with them and fulfill their every request.
They fail to consider the opinions and needs of others, believing their own desires are more important.
“should” statements might sound like this:
• Friends should always help me
• My partner should always support me in everything I do
• My mom should always babysit my kids
• Everything should be exactly how I want it
• I shouldn’t be refused
• The world should be fair to me
If you’ve noticed this kind of thinking in yourself, you likely feel that you deserve success, love, and happiness simply by right of birth.
<q author="Dolly Parton">We can’t direct the wind, but we can adjust the sails.</q>
You expect the universe and the people around you to fulfill your wishes because you are a good, kind person, or because you work hard.

But when this doesn’t happen—and it often doesn’t—you are faced with a choice: sink into gloom and inadequacy, or flare up in anger. People who feel entitled to everything often face significant challenges.

First and foremost, there is frustration: if you are refused, if people don’t understand that they should solve your problems, or if they don’t meet your expectations, you will inevitably face disappointment, resentment, anger, and a sense of being misunderstood. You’ll wonder how anyone could treat such a wonderful person this way.

You spend massive amounts of energy on negative emotions, seeing the world in gloomy tones. Your demanding attitude toward life prevents you from enjoying it or finding joy, because you don’t accept the world as it is; you always have grievances about how it is structured.

Tanya is a clear example of someone with an “everyone owes me” mindset. She expects her friends to always be available, ready to drop everything and rush to her aid, solving her every problem and meeting her every demand.
For example, she might call at 3 a.m., demanding that a friend come over immediately to support her after an argument with her boyfriend.

Or, without any warning, she might ask for help moving, even though her friend already has an important meeting planned for that day. When her friends can’t help, Tanya feels offended, abandoned, and unneeded.
This is a dangerous position that can lead to isolation, tension in relationships, or even the breakdown of those relationships.

Friends and loved ones may start avoiding meetings or conversations, fearing the next demand, resentment, or argument. No one wants to constantly feel obligated or forced to cater to someone else’s whims.
Where does this belief come from? This mindset often forms in childhood when a child isn’t exposed to realistic boundaries and gets everything they want. This can happen for several reasons:
• Parents spoil the child and let them do whatever they want.
In such cases, a narcissistic part of the personality can develop, characterized by an inflated sense of self-importance.

Example: Little Katya always got everything she wanted. Her parents believed she deserved only the best and never said no to her. Katya grew up used to the world revolving around her, and she couldn’t understand why her teachers at school didn’t give her all their attention or why her classmates didn’t defer to her opinion.
• Parents themselves live by the “everyone owes me” principle.
<q author="Osho">No one owes you anything. Everything you receive in life is a gift.</q>
The child repeats the parental pattern, internalizing this way of thinking.

Example: Vanya’s parents constantly complained about life, feeling they should be paid more, that they weren’t appreciated, and that their rights were constantly being violated. Vanya grew up in an atmosphere of dissatisfaction and the expectation that the world owes him something.
Parents didn’t consider the child’s opinion, ignoring their interests and desires.

The child feels angry with their parents but can’t express it openly. As a result, they project this anger onto those around them, believing that others should pity them and compensate for what they lacked in childhood.
Example: Anya always dreamed of becoming an artist, but her parents forced her to study law, believing it was a more prestigious profession. Anya gave in, but her heart always longed for creativity.
She felt resentful toward her parents for not letting her realize her dream, and later projected this resentment onto everyone else, believing that they owed her help in finding happiness in life.
The child was forced to please their parents just to be loved. They grew up with the belief that love must be earned.

Example: Sergey always tried to meet all of his parents’ needs, fearing they wouldn’t love him if he did something wrong. He grew up feeling insecure and constantly tried to prove his worth, believing that he was owed what he deserved.
The consequences of this mindset can be diverse and negative. They include:
• Frustration and dissatisfaction: Expecting others to meet all your needs can lead to constant frustration and a sense of dissatisfaction due to the gap between your expectations and reality
• Relationship tension: The belief that the world should adapt to you can cause tension and conflict in relationships, as it often leads to discontent and disagreements
• Loss of independence: Constantly expecting others to take on all responsibilities makes you dependent and hinders your autonomy and personal growth
• Negative impact on self-esteem: By relying on others to meet your needs, you fail to develop your own self-esteem, which can lead to negative emotions and feelings of inadequacy
• Lack of mutual support: By focusing only on yourself, you miss the opportunity to be empathetic and help others, which can hinder the development of healthy relationships and social support
<q author="Aristotle">Do not expect the world to revolve around you. There is room in this world for others as well</q>

exercise.title: How to deal with “should” statements?
exercise.description: This article explores “should” statements as a source of stress and dissatisfaction, highlighting how these beliefs can make us feel like hostages to our circumstances. The author suggests recognizing the unrealistic nature of such beliefs, replacing them with more flexible language, and taking responsibility for your own desires and actions. Practicing gratitude and compassion, as well as learning to ask for help and accepting imperfection, can help reduce stress and improve your quality of life.

texts: “Should” statements are a silent enemy that steals our joy, undermines our peace of mind, and makes it harder to build healthy, close relationships with those around us.
At the core of this mindset is the idea of obligation.
In most cases, the word “should” itself is a linguistic trap.

The meaning of “should” implies that things must be exactly this way and no other. Phrases like “must,” “obligated,” or “necessary” make us feel like hostages to our circumstances because they imply a situation where no alternative exists.
However, such a definition is only accurate in very rare, almost exceptional cases.
For example, it is realistic to say “a person must breathe air,” because there is physically no alternative.
But saying “no one should be late” is inaccurate and unrealistic, as being late is actually quite possible. People do run late, get delayed, or fail to show up entirely.
Therefore, holding “should” beliefs inevitably leads to acute or chronic stress.
How to break free from “should” statements?
Recognize the unreality of your belief
<q author="Buddha">If you think the world owes you something, it will be a source of your pain. Remember, the world owes no one anything.</q>
By demanding that others behave a certain way, or say and do specific things, you are expecting only one specific outcome from them.
This is a powerful source of stress because no one lives in an environment that always meets their expectations.
Even the most powerful leaders have dealt with people who acted “not as they should.”
Naturally, when we encounter someone acting “not as they should,” our emotional arousal increases. This can lead to constant stress, resentment, and a wide range of negative emotions.
Identify the roots of the belief

Think about where this belief came from. Perhaps you weren’t given realistic boundaries as a child, or you inherited this way of thinking from your parents. Understanding the cause won’t make the belief disappear, but it is an important step in working through it.
Pay attention to how you speak. Track words like “should,” “must,” or “have to” in your speech, and try replacing them with “I want,” “I prefer,” or “I would like.”
Example: Replace “My friends should call me first” with “I would like my friends to call me first.”
Take responsibility
The semantic meaning of these words determines how you relate to a situation.

In one case, it’s an inevitable necessity where responsibility lies with an external force (people, nature, circumstances, etc.); in the other, it’s a free choice where the responsibility lies with you.
It can be hard to take responsibility for your choices, but this path increases your sense of freedom and reduces stress in the long run.
Break down your “should” statements
Instead of saying “they should...”, ask yourself:
• Why do I believe it has to be this way?
• Are there alternative options?
• What am I actually trying to achieve?
• How would it be helpful if it were this way?
Identify your true desires and be honest with yourself. What do you really want when you say someone or something owes you? What values are you protecting?
Learn to ask for and express your needs
Instead of assuming others know what you need or want, learn to express yourself clearly and openly, and ask for help when you need it.
Practice compassion
Try to understand how others feel. Remember that everyone has their own concerns, and they may not always be able to support you, listen to you, praise you, or provide the help you need.
Try to put yourself in other people’s shoes and look for alternative explanations for what is happening; this helps you develop empathy.
Be grateful
Instead of focusing on what others should be doing for you, focus on being grateful for what they do.

For example, imagine a colleague is helping you with a project even though they are very busy. Instead of thinking, “They should be helping me; it’s their job,” reframe your thought to: “I’m grateful for my colleague’s help, especially since they’re so busy. They are a true professional.”

Practicing gratitude helps us notice and appreciate the kindness of others, creating an atmosphere of mutual respect and support. Gratitude can be expressed both personally and publicly, and it helps strengthen our relationships with those around us.
Embrace imperfection
The world isn’t perfect, so don’t demand the impossible from yourself or others. Don’t try to change the world or other people to fit your own mold—it won’t lead to anything good.
Letting go of unhelpful beliefs is a long and not always easy process. But it’s worth it; gradually, you’ll start to feel like a freer, happier, and more confident person.
